scope: Static review of file handling, resource bounds, data safety, and failure behavior.

findings.title: Unbounded whole-file reads can exhaust memory
findings.evidence: read_text loads the full input before DictReader builds a second in-memory row list; validation then reads the output again.
findings.impact: A very large or attacker-supplied CSV can exhaust process memory and terminate the job before a validated output is produced.
findings.assumptions: Relevant when file size is not constrained by a trusted caller or upload layer.
findings.remediation: Enforce a byte-size and row-count limit, sample only the prefix needed by Sniffer, and stream rows through a bounded or disk-backed key store when large inputs are supported.

findings.title: Spreadsheet formulas are preserved in exported cells
findings.evidence: Rows are copied verbatim, so cells beginning with =, +, -, or @ remain formulas when opened by spreadsheet software.
findings.impact: A recipient who opens untrusted output in a spreadsheet may execute formula behavior or follow attacker-controlled links supported by that application.
findings.assumptions: Relevant only when untrusted CSV data is later opened in formula-capable spreadsheet software.
findings.remediation: Offer an explicit spreadsheet-safe mode that prefixes formula-leading cells with an apostrophe, document the semantic change, and keep raw-preservation mode available for non-spreadsheet pipelines.

findings.title: Direct output writes can leave a partial file
findings.evidence: The destination is truncated and written before validation; an exception or process interruption can leave a partial destination at the requested path.
findings.impact: Downstream automation may consume an incomplete file if it watches the destination path concurrently or after a failed run.
findings.assumptions: Relevant when the destination is consumed by another process or replaces a prior good artifact.
findings.remediation: Write to a temporary file in the destination directory, flush and fsync it, validate the temporary file, then atomically replace the destination.

findings.title: Input and output identity is checked before the write
findings.evidence: The resolve-based equality check and the later output open are separate operations, so a concurrently changed symlink can invalidate the earlier check.
findings.impact: In a privileged multi-user wrapper, a local attacker who can mutate path components may redirect the write toward the input or another writable file.
findings.assumptions: Not a practical issue for a single-user CLI invocation; relevant only with untrusted writable path components and concurrent mutation.
findings.remediation: For privileged or multi-user use, reject symlinks, open directory/file descriptors with no-follow semantics, and perform atomic output replacement within a trusted directory.
